column2: This document evaluates the reconstruction and widening of approximately 4.6 miles of Lincoln Highway (U.S. Route 30) from Cicero Avenue to Chicago Road in Cook County, Illinois, at an estimated cost of about $13.2 million. The project passes through Chicago Heights, Matteson, Olympia Fields, and Park Forest, requiring acquisition of eight structures (six commercial and two residential), frontage land from Roosevelt School, and a 0.17-acre temporary easement from the Woodrow Wilson Woods Forest Preserve. Alternatives considered included a no-build option, north or south relocations, and two on-alignment options (A and B), with Alignment A selected as the most feasible and prudent. Principal environmental impacts include displacement of structures, predicted noise levels exceeding FHWA design year standards at most studied sites, and minor temporary use of Section 4(f) land, while air and water quality impacts were found to be insignificant. Public response at the June 20, 1972 hearing and from reviewing agencies was generally favorable, with strong local support and no major unresolved objections.

column2: The project involves reconstruction of approximately 4.6 miles of U.S. Route 30 (Lincoln Highway) from Cicero Avenue to Chicago Road in Cook County, Illinois, widening it from a four-lane undivided highway to six lanes between Cicero and Western Avenues and four lanes from Western Avenue to Chicago Road, with a sixteen-foot mountable median and closed drainage system. The project also includes replacement of the bridge over Thorn Creek, a railroad grade separation, two pedestrian overpasses, and intersection improvements. The total estimated cost is approximately $13.18 million, to be carried out under five contracts.

column2: The improvement passes through the City of Chicago Heights and the Villages of Park Forest, Matteson, and Olympia Fields in Cook County, about 25 miles south of the Chicago Loop, in a heavily urbanized corridor of residential and commercial development. The four communities differ in income, with Olympia Fields having a 1970 median family income of $29,781 and Chicago Heights $11,153. Eight structures (six commercial and two residential) will be acquired, frontage land will be taken from Roosevelt School, and a temporary easement is required from the 31-acre Woodrow Wilson Woods Forest Preserve.

column2: Alternatives considered included not improving the facility (no-build), other modes such as rail or bus rapid transit (rejected due to low population density), relocating the highway north or south of its present alignment, and two on-alignment options. Alignment A places the new centerline along the existing centerline, while Alignment B would shift right-of-way takings to one side; Alignment B was dropped because intervening development made it no longer feasible. Alignment A was recommended as the most feasible and prudent alternative and was the only alignment presented at the public hearing. Four schemes (A–D) were also developed for handling Sunnyside Avenue at Roosevelt School, with Scheme A unanimously selected.

column2: The project will require approximately 16.2 acres of right-of-way and demolition of eight structures (six commercial and two residential), along with 0.20 acres from Roosevelt School and a 0.17-acre temporary easement from the Cook County Forest Preserve. Predicted 1990 design-year L10 noise levels exceed FHWA standards at 46 of 49 Category C sites and 26 of 28 Category B sites, and exceptions to the noise standards will be requested. Carbon monoxide concentrations remain well below the federal standards of 35 PPM (1-hr) and 9 PPM (8-hr), and groundwater quality is expected to be unaffected because of the closed drainage system. Five box culverts designed for a 50-year storm will help alleviate upstream flooding, and disturbed Forest Preserve land will be regraded, topsoiled, fertilized, and sodded to original condition. No National Register sites, unique wetlands, or important wildlife habitats are affected.

column2: A public hearing was held on June 20, 1972 at the O.W. Huth Upper Grade Center in Matteson, Illinois, with public response generally favorable, though residents raised concerns about screen plantings, signalization, access points, drainage, bike paths, and street lighting. The Village of Park Forest passed a resolution on November 13, 1972 to use Motor Fuel Tax Funds to pay for replacement screen plantings, and local officials including the Mayor of Chicago Heights, the Village of Park Forest, and State Senator Don A. Moore strongly supported the project. Federal and state reviewing agencies—including the Department of the Interior, HUD, EPA, the Northeastern Illinois Planning Commission, and the Cook County Forest Preserve District—raised no major objections, with NIPC finding the project consistent with regional plans and Interior concurring on the Section 4(f) determination.
